entry.title: [OctoPrint] OctoPrint: Stored XSS via saved connection parameters
entry.content:
Impact

OctoPrint versions 2.0.0rc1 up until version 2.0.0rc6 are susceptible to cross-site scripting via a specially crafted default port or baudrate setting on the bundled Serial Connector plugin, supplied via the API as new defaults during a connect request.

Patches

The vulnerability is patched in 2.0.0rc7.

Workaround

Check config.yaml for Javascript fragments in printerConnection.preferred.parameters.port or printerConnection.preferred.parameters.baudrate. If found, remove them. You can check who of your users had access to your instance since you flashed 2.0.0rc1 or above via auth.log.

Credits

This vulnerability was discovered and responsibly disclosed to OctoPrint by "mahn-don".

Timeline

2026-10-14: Report received 2026-10-14: Report acknowledged 2026-10-14: Report verified 2026-10-14: Fix ready for 2.0.0rc7 2026-10-20: CVE requested

entry.title: [compose-lint] compose-lint: Incomplete fix for GHSA-jf3h-8jvx-vcrg: a run stopped at the finding limit quotes a secret from a CI-generated `.env`
entry.content:
Impact

This is an incomplete fix for GHSA-jf3h-8jvx-vcrg. 0.32.0 made findings quote the ${NAME} a sibling .env filled in, instead of its value. The same release added a stop at 20,000 findings per document, and that stop is checked before the quoting step. A run that hits it reports the findings graded so far with the resolved values still in them, in text, JSON and SARIF output. That happens with or without --allow-partial-coverage.

The attack is the one GHSA-jf3h-8jvx-vcrg describes. In a CI workflow that writes secrets into the .env beside the Compose file, a pull request changes a line to image: "${DB_PASSWORD}". It also pushes the document past 20,000 findings, which a few hundred lines can do, because an aliased list is graded once for each service that uses it. The secret's value is quoted in a finding that reaches the job log, the JSON output and the SARIF uploaded to Code Scanning. GitHub masks registered secrets in the job log, but not in uploaded JSON or SARIF artifacts or in Code Scanning alert text. The run exits 2, or 0 with --allow-partial-coverage, after the output has been written.

The preconditions are the same as for GHSA-jf3h-8jvx-vcrg. The workflow writes secrets into the .env beside the Compose file and runs on pull requests from authors who should not see them, such as a pull_request_target workflow that lints the pull request's files. Pull requests from forks normally run without secrets, so the common setup is not exposed. The inflated document is visible in the pull request, but the workflow runs before anyone reviews it.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

Python package. compose-lint 0.32.0. Earlier releases have no finding limit, and their quoting gap is GHSA-jf3h-8jvx-vcrg itself.

GitHub Action. Action tag v0.32.0 is affected. Tags before v0.22.0 install the newest release unless version: is set, so they currently install 0.32.0.

pre-commit hook. rev: v0.32.0.

Docker image. composelint/compose-lint:0.32.0, :0.32 and latest are affected when the .env is mounted with the project.

Patches

No fixed release yet.

Workarounds

  • Run with --no-env, which skips the sibling .env.
  • Don't write secrets into the .env beside the Compose file in a job that lints untrusted pull requests.

Reproduction

project/.env          DB_PASSWORD=example-secret      (written by CI, not committed)
project/compose.yml   x-p: &p [ ...200 port mappings... ]
                      services: one service with image: "${DB_PASSWORD}" and ports: *p,
                                plus about 100 more services with ports: *p

compose-lint --format sarif compose.yml exits 2 with "grading stopped at 20000 findings", and the reported findings contain example-secret. The same file with fewer services stays under the limit and quotes ${DB_PASSWORD}. Checked against the 0.32.0 wheel from PyPI, using a synthetic value.

entry.title: [gpustack] GPUStack: Missing authorization on several cluster and resource endpoints allows cross-user access and cluster takeover
entry.content:
Impact

An authenticated non-administrative user could access a Kubernetes cluster they are not authorized to access through GPUStack's Kubernetes API proxy.

The cluster_apiserver_proxy handler did not perform a resource-level authorization check before forwarding requests to the selected cluster. Requests were forwarded through a worker using its Kubernetes ServiceAccount credentials.

Depending on the permissions granted to that ServiceAccount, an attacker could read sensitive Kubernetes resources, create or modify workloads, or delete resources and disrupt services. Creating attacker-controlled workloads could result in code execution in the target cluster.

Exploitation requires a Kubernetes-provider cluster with a reachable worker. The operations available to the attacker are limited by the worker's ServiceAccount permissions.

Patches

Fixed in gpustack v2.2.2.

Workarounds

Restrict access to the GPUStack instance to trusted administrator accounts until upgrading.

References

  • https://github.com/gpustack/gpustack/security/advisories/GHSA-3hch-x692-6qj3
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-103002

entry.title: [gpustack] GPUStack: SAML callback trusts an unverified SAMLResponse, allowing authentication bypass and account takeover
entry.content:
Impact

The callback Base64-decodes the posted XML, reads NameID and attributes, resolves or provisions the user, and mints a gpustack_session JWT — but never calls OneLogin_Saml2_Auth.process_response(), the step that verifies the signature, issuer, audience, destination, and time conditions.

No credentials are required, and SAML SSO does not even need to be configured. The callback processes the payload and issues a session regardless of whether SAML is set up, so every deployment is affected, not only SAML-enabled ones. Anyone who can reach the endpoint over the network can authenticate as an arbitrary identity by posting a response that names it:

  • If the name matches an existing user (e.g. an administrator), the attacker receives that user's session — full account takeover, including administrator access.
  • Otherwise, a new non-admin user is provisioned.

Administrator access grants full control over the deployment and the infrastructure it manages. Because Response/Assertion IDs are never consumed, a captured signed response also replays indefinitely.

Precondition: network reachability to /auth/saml/callback. SAML SSO configuration is not required. A full proof-of-concept is available privately to maintainers.

Patches

Fixed in gpustack 2.2.2:

  • The SAML callback now validates the response via OneLogin_Saml2_Auth.process_response() — signature, issuer, audience, destination, and time conditions — and rejects responses that fail, so forged or replayed assertions are no longer accepted.
  • The SAML and OIDC login/callback routes are now gated to run only when that provider is the configured active provider, so a deployment that has not enabled the provider no longer parses attacker-supplied IdP payloads.

Workarounds

There is no effective configuration-level workaround — disabling or not configuring SAML does not mitigate this on affected versions, since the callback runs regardless. Until upgraded, block network access to /auth/saml/callback (e.g. at a reverse proxy / ingress).

Credit

Reported privately by Austin Chu, Sohee Kim, and Corban Villa (UC Berkeley security research project), and independently, earlier, by a researcher who wishes to remain anonymous.

References

  • https://github.com/gpustack/gpustack/security/advisories/GHSA-62m9-f875-rqw6

entry.title: [autogen] AG2: Newline injection in SandboxShellTool bypasses allowed=[...] and readonly=True, enabling arbitrary command execution
entry.content:
Summary

SandboxShellTool's restricted modes — allowed=[...] (explicit command allowlist) and readonly=True (implicit READONLY_COMMANDS allowlist) — can both be bypassed by embedding a newline character inside the command string. The filter only inspects a single-line set of shell metacharacters, but execution runs the raw string through sh -c, where a shell treats an embedded newline exactly like a ; statement separator. An agent (or content that steers the agent, e.g. via prompt injection) can therefore run arbitrary shell commands even when the tool was configured to allow only a specific command prefix or only read-only commands. With the default LocalEnvironment() backend this is a real host subprocess (its own docstring: "Commands run via subprocess on the host, so there is no real isolation"), not an isolated container, so this is full host command execution, not merely an escape from an already-sandboxed environment.

Details

Both restricted modes are enforced by ShellAdapter._filter() in ag2/tools/sandbox/adapter/shell.py:

def _filter(self, command: str) -> str | None:
    if self._allowed is not None:
        if not any(matches(p, command) for p in self._allowed):
            return f"Command not allowed: {command!r}"
        if contains_shell_operator(command):
            return f"Command not allowed (shell operators are not permitted in restricted mode): {command!r}"
    ...

readonly=True reuses this exact same branch: SandboxShellTool.__init__ / ShellAdapter.__init__ sets self._allowed = list(READONLY_COMMANDS) when readonly is set and no explicit allowed is given, so both modes share one filter and one bypass.

contains_shell_operator() in ag2/tools/sandbox/filter.py checks the command against:

_SHELL_OPERATORS: tuple[str, ...] = (">", ">>", "|", ";", "&&", "||", "`", "$(")

This tuple has no entry for \n (or \r). matches() only checks that the command starts with an allowed prefix followed by a space or end-of-string; it never inspects the remainder of the string. Execution is:

argv = ["sh", "-c", command]
...
return await sandbox.exec(argv, env=self._env, timeout=self._timeout)

A POSIX shell splits sh -c "<line1>\n<line2>" into two sequential statements, the same as if they were separated by ;. So a command such as "cat allowed_file.txt\nrm -rf /anything":

  1. Passes matches("cat", command) — the string starts with "cat ".
    1. Passes contains_shell_operator(command) — \n is not a recognized operator.
    1. Reaches sh -c "cat allowed_file.txt\nrm -rf /anything", which runs both statements.

Proof of Concept

Verified directly against the current main branch (github.com/ag2ai/ag2, commit a05ff1cb6ff4955ef252a4e0d4a27d3a32ad57f0, cloned 2026-09-21), by importing the real ag2/tools/sandbox/filter.py module (stdlib-only, no other AG2 dependencies needed) and reproducing ShellAdapter._filter()'s allowlist branch verbatim:

=== allowed=['cat'] ===
'cat /etc/passwd; rm -rf /tmp/x'   -> Command not allowed (shell operators are not permitted in restricted mode): ...
'cat /etc/passwd && rm -rf /tmp/x' -> Command not allowed (shell operators are not permitted in restricted mode): ...
'cat /etc/passwd | rm -rf /tmp/x'  -> Command not allowed (shell operators are not permitted in restricted mode): ...
'cat /etc/passwd\nrm -rf /tmp/x'   -> None   <-- BYPASS: newline variant is NOT rejected

=== readonly=True (uses READONLY_COMMANDS as the allowed list) ===
'echo hi\nid'                      -> None   <-- BYPASS in readonly mode too

=== sh -c really treats the embedded newline as a second statement (mirrors ShellAdapter._exec_async) ===
$ sh -c 'echo first-command-output\necho SECOND-STATEMENT-RAN-$((21*2))'
first-command-output
SECOND-STATEMENT-RAN-42

The three standard chaining attempts (;, &&, |) are correctly rejected by the real filter, confirming it does real work; the newline-separated variant, expressing the same intent, is accepted by the identical filter in both restricted modes, and a real sh -c call confirms the shell executes both statements.

Impact

Any agent configured with SandboxShellTool(allowed=[...]) or SandboxShellTool(readonly=True) — the two configurations the tool's own docstring presents as actual security boundaries, as opposed to blocked, which the same docstring explicitly says "is not a security boundary" — can be made to execute arbitrary shell commands via a single embedded newline in the command argument. Because tool arguments are LLM-generated and can be steered by content the agent processes (a fetched document, tool output, or any other text reaching the model — i.e. indirect prompt injection), this is reachable without the operator of the agent writing the malicious command themselves. With the default LocalEnvironment() backend, this is command execution on the host process running the agent, not confined to a container.

Suggested Remediation

  • Add "\n" and "\r" to _SHELL_OPERATORS in ag2/tools/sandbox/filter.py so contains_shell_operator() rejects embedded newlines the same way it rejects ;.
    • More robustly, execute allowlisted/readonly commands without invoking a shell in restricted mode (shlex.split + exec with no sh -c wrapper), so redirection, chaining, substitution, and every kind of statement separator are inert by construction instead of relying on an enumerated denylist.

Environment Tested

  • Repository: github.com/ag2ai/ag2, commit a05ff1cb6ff4955ef252a4e0d4a27d3a32ad57f0 (main), cloned 2026-09-21.
    • PyPI package ag2, version 1.0.5 per pyproject.toml on this commit.
    • Python 3, stdlib only (subprocess, importlib) against the real, unmodified ag2/tools/sandbox/filter.py — no AG2 runtime dependencies required to reproduce.

References

  • https://github.com/ag2ai/ag2/security/advisories/GHSA-2h4w-29cv-2cmv
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-113663
  • https://github.com/ag2ai/ag2/commit/3cd86726bb731eb11d6270f0ef9e50e42b5abb39
  • https://github.com/ag2ai/ag2/releases/tag/v1.1.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2h4w-29cv-2cmv

entry.title: [compose-lint] compose-lint: A pull request can make compose-lint quote a secret from a CI-generated `.env` into its findings
entry.content:
Impact

Since 0.22.0, compose-lint fills in ${VAR} references from the .env beside the Compose file, as Compose does. The documentation says values under environment: are never resolved from a .env, "that is where secrets live". But image: values are resolved, and CL-0004 and CL-0019 quote the resolved image in their message and fix text.

Some CI workflows write secrets into that .env before linting or building. In such a workflow, a pull request that changes one line to image: "${DB_PASSWORD}", or image: "nginx:${DB_PASSWORD}", gets the secret's value quoted in a finding. The finding reaches the job log, JSON output, and the SARIF uploaded to Code Scanning. GitHub masks registered secrets in the job log, but not in uploaded JSON or SARIF artifacts or in Code Scanning alert text. The pass/fail result is not affected.

This needs a workflow that writes secrets into the .env beside the Compose file and runs on pull requests from authors who should not see them. Pull requests from forks normally run without secrets, so the common setup is not exposed, which is why this is scored as low confidentiality impact. Where the conditions hold, such as a pull_request_target workflow, pull requests from branches in the same repository, or a self-hosted runner that keeps a populated .env in the checkout, the whole value is disclosed.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

GitHub Action. Action tags v0.22.0 through v0.31.0 install their own compose-lint version and are affected. Earlier tags install the newest release unless version: is set, and so currently install an affected one.

Docker image. composelint/compose-lint tags 0.22.0 through 0.31.0, the matching minor tags, and latest are affected when the .env is mounted with the project.

Patches

Fixed in 0.32.0. Rules still grade the value the sibling .env substituted, but findings, fix guidance and notes quote the ${NAME} reference in its place, in text, JSON and SARIF. A value shorter than 8 characters is shown as written, because short values are also words the guidance itself uses; docs/what-a-run-reads.md states this limit.

Workarounds

  • Upgrade to 0.32.0 or later.
  • Run with --no-env, which skips the sibling .env.
  • Don't write secrets into the .env beside the Compose file in a job that lints untrusted pull requests.

Reproduction

project/.env          DB_PASSWORD=example-secret      (written by CI, not committed)
project/compose.yml   services: {web: {image: "${DB_PASSWORD}"}}

compose-lint --format sarif compose.yml reports CL-0004 with the message Image 'example-secret' has no tag, ....

References

  • https://github.com/tmatens/compose-lint/security/advisories/GHSA-jf3h-8jvx-vcrg
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-123372
  • https://github.com/tmatens/compose-lint/pull/944
  • https://github.com/tmatens/compose-lint/commit/977da9724789264c2662afe47f79220e915442c2
  • https://github.com/tmatens/compose-lint/releases/tag/v0.32.0

entry.title: [compose-lint] compose-lint: `fix --apply` can delete a line the user did not select, including a security setting
entry.content:
Impact

compose-lint fix --apply converts the line numbers its fixers work with into positions in the file. The YAML parser treats a lone carriage return, U+0085, U+2028 and U+2029 as line breaks, but the conversion counted only \n. One of those characters inside a quoted value, which most editors and diff views don't show, shifted every later edit down by one line.

A Compose file from a pull request can use this to make a fix delete the line after the one it meant to change. For example, fixing CL-0014 (logging: driver: none) instead removes driver: none and the following networks: [internal], moving the service off an internal-only network onto the default bridge. The result is still valid Compose, every check fix runs after editing passes, and the command reports applied 1 fix(es) and exits 0. A later compose-lint check passes too, because no rule requires networks:. The dry-run diff (without --apply) does show the removed lines, but --apply prints only the note for the fix that was selected.

A related crash on the same files could empty the SARIF output for every file in the run. GitHub Code Scanning rejects an empty SARIF upload, which fails the step, so that part does not report a false clean result there.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

Docker image. composelint/compose-lint tags 0.9.0 through 0.17.0, and the matching minor tags, are affected when used to run fix --apply. Fixed from 0.18.0.

The GitHub Action does not run fix and is not affected.

Patches

Fixed in 0.18.0. Line splitting and position conversion now share one definition of a line break, so they can't disagree. A Compose file containing an ambiguous line break (a lone \r, U+0085, U+2028 or U+2029) is refused with exit code 2, because no line numbering is correct for both the parser and the editor. CRLF and LF files are unaffected.

Workarounds

  • Upgrade to 0.18.0 or later.
  • On older versions, review the dry-run diff before --apply, and don't run fix --apply over files from untrusted pull requests.

Reproduction

services:
  web:
    image: nginx@sha256:<digest>
    labels:
      note: "line one<U+2028>line two"
    logging:
      driver: none
    networks: [internal]
networks:
  internal:
    internal: true

compose-lint fix --apply compose.yml on 0.17.0 reports applied 1 fix(es), exits 0, and removes both driver: none and networks: [internal].

References

  • https://github.com/tmatens/compose-lint/security/advisories/GHSA-65v8-q222-64xx
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-123370
  • https://github.com/tmatens/compose-lint/pull/547
  • https://github.com/tmatens/compose-lint/pull/549
  • https://github.com/tmatens/compose-lint/commit/c9d453a6a69c076788fe1db05cb54684a616d1de

entry.title: [compose-lint] compose-lint: .env read through a symlink outside the project can expose the CI job's environment
entry.content:
Impact

compose-lint fills in ${VAR} references from the .env file next to the Compose file. It is meant to read nothing outside the project directory, and env_file:, include: and extends: paths are checked for that. The .env read is not. If .env is a symlink, compose-lint follows it wherever it points.

A pull request can add a .env symlink to any file on the CI runner and a Compose file that references a variable from it. compose-lint substitutes the value and quotes it in finding messages, which go to the log and to JSON and SARIF output.

The worst target is /proc/self/environ, the linter's own environment. The Compose file only needs to reference the name of the first variable in it: because that file separates variables with NUL bytes rather than newlines, the substituted value is the entire rest of the environment. On a CI runner that environment holds whatever the workflow put there, including secrets. GitHub masks registered secrets in the job log, but not in uploaded JSON or SARIF artifacts or in Code Scanning alert text.

An include: entry's project_directory: has the same gap from 0.28.0: a directory symlink named there makes compose-lint read .env from wherever the link points.

Pull requests from forks normally run without secrets, and GitHub masks registered secrets in the job log, so in the common setup what can be read is runner metadata and whatever unmasked values the job's environment holds. That is why this is scored as low confidentiality impact. The impact is high in a job that runs untrusted pull requests with secrets in its environment, such as a pull_request_target workflow, or on a CI system that does not mask secrets, and also wherever the JSON or SARIF output is uploaded. The pass/fail result is not affected.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

Patches

Fixed in 0.31.0. Every .env read now applies the same containment check as env_file:. A .env that resolves outside the project is treated as missing and reported as an unread input. A project_directory: that resolves outside the project is refused, and that entry's files resolve against their own directories. A .env line containing a NUL byte is skipped.

Workarounds

  • Run with --no-env, which skips the sibling .env entirely.
  • Don't run compose-lint on untrusted pull requests in a job whose environment holds secrets.

Reproduction

project/.env -> /proc/self/environ      (symlink)
project/compose.yml:
  services:
    web:
      image: "${FIRST_VAR_NAME}"

compose-lint check compose.yml --format json quotes the environment in the CL-0004 message ("Image '...' has no tag").

entry.title: [compose-lint] compose-lint: A committed symlink makes compose-lint quote a file from outside the project into its output
entry.content:
Impact

Like Docker Compose, compose-lint follows symlinks when it reads a project's files. Unlike Compose, compose-lint up to 0.24.0 could then put the contents of a file from outside the project into its output, where the author of a pull request can read it.

A pull request can commit a symlink, under a name compose-lint reads, pointing at a file on the CI runner:

  • The Compose file itself (0.2.0–0.24.0). A compose.yml that is a symlink, whether the pre-commit hook passes its name or the Action or a bare run finds it.
  • compose.override.yml (0.22.0–0.24.0), which compose-lint merges automatically.
  • A COMPOSE_FILE entry (0.22.0–0.24.0) in a .env beside the Compose file.

When the target is not valid YAML, the parse error quotes the line it failed on. Docker Compose, given the same file, reports only a line number. That line reaches standard error (the job log), JSON errors[], and the SARIF toolExecutionNotifications, which the Action uploads to Code Scanning.

A fourth route: from 0.23.0, a symlinked env_file: target makes CL-0020 and CL-0021 report the credential-like key names in a file outside the project. Values are not printed.

What can be read is one line of a file chosen by path, at the point where the YAML parser fails, which the attacker cannot choose; or key names. A symlink to /proc/self/environ gave neither in testing. The pass/fail result is not affected. On a public repository the job log is visible to the pull request's author.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

GitHub Action. Action tags v0.18.0 through v0.24.0 install their own compose-lint version and are affected. Earlier tags install the newest release unless version: is set; they were affected while that was 0.24.0 or earlier.

Docker image. composelint/compose-lint tags 0.3.3 through 0.24.0, and the matching minor tags, are affected. Inside the container a symlink resolves within the container, so what can be read is the container's own files and anything mounted into it. Fixed from 0.25.0.

Patches

Fixed in 0.25.0. Parse errors no longer quote the source line; the error and its line and column are kept. env_file: targets and COMPOSE_FILE entries that resolve outside the project are also refused, with the existing outside-the-project note. Symlinks that stay inside the project still work.

From 0.25.0 through 0.31.0, a committed symlink to a target that is itself a Compose file could still be read, and its values could reach findings. 0.32.0 stops following a discovered, named or override Compose file whose link leaves the checkout.

A related gap for the sibling .env file is covered by GHSA-6wcv-rj3c-mhv3, and one for a symlinked .compose-lint.yml by GHSA-88f4-frh5-gmcr.

Workarounds

  • Upgrade to 0.25.0 or later.
  • On older versions, don't run compose-lint on untrusted pull requests on a machine whose files outside the checkout hold credentials. --no-env closes the COMPOSE_FILE and env_file: routes, but not the others.

Reproduction

project/compose.yml -> /path/outside/project/credentials   (symlink)

compose-lint --format sarif compose.yml on 0.24.0 exits 2, and the SARIF notification quotes a line of the linked file. On 0.25.0 the error gives only the line and column.

entry.title: [compose-lint] compose-lint: Compose file text can issue GitHub Actions workflow commands through the compose-lint Action
entry.content:
Impact

The GitHub Actions runner treats certain text in a step's output as commands. The legacy form, ##[command], is recognized anywhere in a line. compose-lint's text report prints service names, environment keys and lines of the Compose file, and it does not neutralize ##[. Inside the compose-lint Action, a Compose file from a pull request can therefore:

  • create fake error or warning annotations on the pull request (##[error], ##[warning])
  • fold the rest of the log, including the real verdict, out of sight (##[group])
  • blank out chosen strings for the rest of the log (##[add-mask])

GitHub has postponed removing the deprecated set-output log command, so the runner still honors it. A test run of the Action on a GitHub-hosted runner confirmed that a ::set-output line from a Compose file is processed. Whether it can override the Action's own sarif-written output, which decides whether the SARIF upload step runs, has not been tested.

The exit code and the pass/fail result are not affected. Azure Pipelines parses the same ##[ syntax, so the pip package is listed for anyone printing the text report in other CI systems.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

Patches

Fixed in 0.31.0. The Action stops the runner from processing workflow commands while compose-lint's output is printed, using a random stop-commands token. The text report also escapes ##[, and :: at the start of a line, in anything taken from the Compose file.

Workarounds

  • In your own workflow, wrap the compose-lint step in ::stop-commands::<random token> and ::<random token>::.
  • Use --format json or --format sarif rather than the text report when linting untrusted pull requests.

Reproduction

services:
  web:
    image: "nginx:1.25"
    environment:
      "##[error]DB_PASSWORD": placeholder
  "##[group]svc":
    image: "nginx:1.25"
    privileged: true

Run through the Action, this produces a fake error annotation and folds the remaining log lines, including the FAIL verdict, into a collapsed group.

entry.title: [compose-lint] compose-lint: A `.compose-lint.yml` symlinked outside the project is read, and a parse error quotes part of the target
entry.content:
Impact

compose-lint automatically reads a .compose-lint.yml policy file beside the Compose file. It is meant to read nothing outside the project directory, but it follows that file if it is a symlink, wherever it points.

A pull request can commit .compose-lint.yml as a symlink to a file on the CI runner. If the target is not valid YAML, the error compose-lint reports quotes part of the line the parser failed on. That quote reaches the job log (standard error), JSON errors[], and the SARIF toolExecutionNotifications, which the Action uploads to Code Scanning. The run exits 2.

What can be read is small. The quote is cut to about 30 characters around the error position, and the attacker cannot choose which line of the target the parser fails on. For an INI-style credentials file, this was the start of the second line (aws_access_key_id = followed by the first characters of the value). Targets in KEY=value form, and YAML files that parse, disclosed no values in testing. The pass/fail result is not affected. On a public repository, the job log is visible to the pull request's author.

The Compose file loader stopped quoting source lines in parse errors in 0.25.0 (GHSA-whr6-fgpq-fpv9). The policy loader did not.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

GitHub Action. Action tags v0.18.0 through v0.31.0 install their own compose-lint version and are affected. Earlier tags install the newest release unless version: is set, and so currently install an affected one.

Docker image. composelint/compose-lint tags 0.3.3 through 0.31.0, the matching minor tags, and latest are affected. Inside the container, a symlink resolves within the container, so what can be read is the container's own files and anything mounted into it.

Patches

Fixed in 0.32.0. A .compose-lint.yml discovered in the working directory that resolves outside it is refused with exit 2 rather than read, and a policy parse error no longer quotes the line it failed on, matching the Compose loader. --config is read as given. 0.32.0 also stops following a Compose file that is a symlink to a target outside the checkout.

Workarounds

  • Upgrade to 0.32.0 or later.
  • Run with an explicit --config pointing at a policy file inside the project; the automatic lookup is then skipped.
  • Don't run compose-lint on untrusted pull requests on a machine whose files outside the checkout hold credentials.

Reproduction

project/.compose-lint.yml -> /path/outside/project/credentials   (symlink)

compose-lint --format sarif compose.yml exits 2, and the notification text quotes the start of the target's second line.

entry.title: [kiwitcms] Kiwi TCMS account confirmation open redirect through protocol-relative URLs
entry.content:
Summary

In Kiwi TCMS version 16.1, the fix for CVE-2026-54724 (open redirect via unvalidated next parameter) in the account confirmation endpoint is incomplete. The validation uses startswith("/") to check if the redirect URL is local, but this is bypassed by protocol-relative URLs like //evil.com which start with / but redirect the browser to an external attacker-controlled domain. 16.1’s incomplete mitigation still allows protocol-relative destinations and earlier releases lack the mitigation.

Vulnerable Code

In tcms/kiwi_auth/views.py, the Confirm view (line ~113):

def get_redirect_url(self, *args, **kwargs):
    self.url = self.request.GET.get("next", reverse("core-views-index"))
    if not self.url.startswith("/"):
        self.url = reverse("core-views-index")

The check startswith("/") passes for //evil.com because it begins with /, but browsers interpret //evil.com as a protocol-relative URL that redirects to https://evil.com (or http://evil.com depending on the current page's protocol).

Proof of Concept

GET /confirm/<activation_key>/?next=//evil.com/phishing HTTP/1.1
Host: kiwi.example.com

Response:

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: //evil.com/phishing

The browser follows the redirect to https://evil.com/phishing.

Verification:

>>> url = "//evil.com/phishing"
>>> url.startswith("/")
True  # passes the check!

Impact

An attacker can craft a confirmation link that, after the user confirms their account, redirects them to a phishing page. This is useful for:

  • Credential phishing (fake login page on attacker domain)
  • Malware delivery after trusted action
  • Social engineering (user trusts the link because it's from the legitimate Kiwi TCMS instance)

The attack requires sending a crafted activation link to a user who is registering, or intercepting/predicting the activation key.

Suggested Fix

Use Django's url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme() utility instead of a simple startswith check:

from django.utils.http import url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme

def get_redirect_url(self, *args, **kwargs):
    self.url = self.request.GET.get("next", reverse("core-views-index"))
    if not url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme(
        self.url,
        allowed_hosts={self.request.get_host()},
        require_https=self.request.is_secure(),
    ):
        self.url = reverse("core-views-index")

This properly rejects protocol-relative URLs, absolute URLs to other hosts, and other bypass patterns.

Fixed in Version 16.2

entry.title: [code-graph-rag] Code Graph RAG structural tools follow out-of-root symlinks
entry.content:
A remote/local attacker who can get a symbolic link included in a source-code repository that code-graph-rag analyzes can cause the structural_search and structural_replace tools (backed by AstGrepService, exposed both as MCP tools and as agentic AI tools) to read and -- via structural_replace with dry_run=False -- overwrite arbitrary files outside the configured project root, because the tool's path-containment check (should_skip_path/_classify_file) is performed lexically on the unresolved path and never checks Path.is_symlink() or calls .resolve(), unlike the project's own (correct) validate_project_path decorator used elsewhere.

Tested at commit 90a3ed3cbdc7d3bb8036985b851cc7c9a3ba9c57 (pyproject version 0.0.550), current main at test time. Confirmed this commit already contains the fix for the prior advisory (GHSA-vvr2-h2jp-838m: paginated read_file path traversal) and the newer HTTP-MCP bearer-auth gate (_validate_http_exposure in codebase_rag/mcp/server.py) -- this is a distinct, still-open issue on top of those fixes, in a different component with a different root cause and a strictly worse impact (write, not just read).

Details

AstGrepService (codebase_rag/tools/ast_grep_service.py) backs both the structural_search and structural_replace MCP/agentic tools. It enumerates candidate files with os.walk() and gates each path only through should_skip_path():

  • codebase_rag/tools/ast_grep_service.py:84-109 (_iter_source_files) -- walks self.project_root with os.walk(); every non-directory dirent returned (including a symlink pointing anywhere on disk) is treated as an in-scope file.
  • codebase_rag/tools/ast_grep_service.py:61-82 (_classify_file) -- the only containment check is should_skip_path(...) followed by abs_path.relative_to(self.project_root) (line 82); abs_path is never resolved, so this check is purely lexical/string-based.
  • codebase_rag/utils/path_utils.py:80-109 (should_skip_path) and codebase_rag/utils/path_utils.py:35-37 (cached_relative_path) -- computes rel_path = file_path.relative_to(repo_path) without ever calling .resolve() or Path.is_symlink().
  • Read sink: codebase_rag/tools/ast_grep_service.py:143-144 (search) -- source = self._read(abs_path) calls path.read_text(), which Python follows through the symlink to its real target.
  • Write sink: codebase_rag/tools/ast_grep_service.py:187-208 (replace), line 208 -- abs_path.write_text(new_source, ...) when dry_run=False, again following the symlink and overwriting the real target file's content.

This is inconsistent with how the rest of the codebase handles the exact same class of risk. The file read/write/edit tools (file_reader.py, file_writer.py, file_editor.py) are all protected by validate_project_path (codebase_rag/decorators.py:73-75):

full_path = (self.project_root / file_path_str).resolve()
project_root = self.project_root.resolve()
full_path.relative_to(project_root)

.resolve() follows symlinks before the containment check runs, so those tools correctly reject an out-of-root target. path_utils.py's own absolute_path_within_project_root() (codebase_rag/utils/path_utils.py:156-176) documents the same principle explicitly in its docstring: "The resolve() calls are load-bearing: containment is checked lexically, so an unresolved .. segment or symlink would escape the root." -- but should_skip_path()/AstGrepService never applies that pattern.

Reachability: structural_search (codebase_rag/tools/structural_search.py:24-46) carries no requires_approval flag at all -- in AI-orchestrator mode the model can call it autonomously with no human confirmation. structural_replace (codebase_rag/tools/structural_editor.py:52-57) is marked requires_approval=True, but that flag is only enforced by pydantic-ai's own agent loop -- the MCP server path bypasses it entirely: MCPToolsRegistry.structural_replace (codebase_rag/mcp/tools.py:586-596) calls self._structural_editor_tool.function(...) directly, registered with no approval concept at codebase_rag/mcp/tools.py:369-388. Any MCP client that can call tools can invoke structural_replace with dry_run=False in one shot.

Proof of Concept

Dynamically confirmed against the installed package (mgclient/pymgclient mocked, as in the prior advisory's own PoC, since the Memgraph native client isn't needed for this code path).

mkdir -p /tmp/poc_symlink/safe-project-root
cat > /tmp/poc_symlink/outside-secret.py << 'EOF'
API_TOKEN = "sk-live-EXAMPLE-NOT-A-REAL-SECRET-1234567890"
def get_token():
    return API_TOKEN
EOF
ln -s /tmp/poc_symlink/outside-secret.py /tmp/poc_symlink/safe-project-root/linked_module.py

import sys
from pathlib import Path
from unittest.mock import MagicMock
sys.modules["mgclient"] = MagicMock()
sys.modules["pymgclient"] = MagicMock()
from codebase_rag.tools.ast_grep_service import AstGrepService

SAFE_ROOT = "/tmp/poc_symlink/safe-project-root"
svc = AstGrepService(project_root=SAFE_ROOT)

matches = svc.search(pattern="API_TOKEN", language="python")
# -> match in reported file='linked_module.py' text='API_TOKEN'  (read escape)

changes = svc.replace(pattern="API_TOKEN", rewrite="PWNED_BY_STRUCTURAL_REPLACE",
                       language="python", dry_run=False)
print(Path("/tmp/poc_symlink/outside-secret.py").read_text())

Actual run output:

[*] Calling AstGrepService.search('API_TOKEN', language='python') ...
    match in reported file='linked_module.py' text='API_TOKEN'
    match in reported file='linked_module.py' text='API_TOKEN'
[+] READ ESCAPE CONFIRMED: content of the out-of-root file was returned by
    structural_search(), attributed to a path 'inside' the project root.

[*] Calling AstGrepService.replace(pattern='API_TOKEN',
    rewrite='PWNED_BY_STRUCTURAL_REPLACE', dry_run=False) ...
    wrote change to reported file='linked_module.py' matches=2

[*] Outside file content AFTER structural_replace:
------------------------------------------------------------
# Simulated sensitive file OUTSIDE the analyzed project root
PWNED_BY_STRUCTURAL_REPLACE = "sk-live-EXAMPLE-NOT-A-REAL-SECRET-1234567890"

def get_token():
    return PWNED_BY_STRUCTURAL_REPLACE
------------------------------------------------------------
[+] WRITE ESCAPE CONFIRMED: a file OUTSIDE the configured project_root
    (/tmp/poc_symlink/safe-project-root) was modified by structural_replace
    via a symlink placed inside the root.

Impact

Any operator who points cgr (CLI, agentic ask_agent mode, or MCP structural_search/structural_replace tools) at a repository they did not fully audit -- the exact use case this tool is built for ("query, understand, and edit multi-language codebases") -- can have that repository's planted symlink used to:

  • Disclose the contents of any file readable by the cgr process (credentials, SSH keys, .env files, sibling project source), via structural_search, with no approval gate at all.
  • Overwrite the contents of any file writable by the cgr process, via structural_replace(dry_run=False), bypassing the tool's own approval gate when called through the MCP protocol.

Remediation

Apply the same resolve-then-contain pattern already used by validate_project_path (codebase_rag/decorators.py:73-75) and absolute_path_within_project_root (codebase_rag/utils/path_utils.py:156-176) to should_skip_path. Reject any path whose resolved (symlink-followed) location escapes the resolved project root:

--- a/codebase_rag/utils/path_utils.py
+++ b/codebase_rag/utils/path_utils.py
@@ def should_skip_path(
     _is_file = path.is_file() if is_file is None else is_file
     if _is_file and path.suffix in cs.IGNORE_SUFFIXES:
         return True
+    # Reject symlinks (or any path) that resolve outside the project root,
+    # mirroring validate_project_path's decorator (decorators.py:73-75) and
+    # absolute_path_within_project_root (this module, below).
+    try:
+        path.resolve().relative_to(repo_path.resolve())
+    except ValueError:
+        return True
     rel_path = cached_relative_path(path, repo_path)

Concretely: this one change in should_skip_path fixes both _classify_file (search) and the os.walk filtering in _iter_source_files (replace), since both route through it. As defense in depth, _iter_source_files could additionally skip symlinked dirents outright (entry.is_symlink()) during the os.walk.

Credit: Dostxodjayev Abdullox (GitHub: squeeze440)

References

  • https://github.com/vitali87/code-graph-rag/commit/2648c95aa550ce2d9361a8e75ed669d5f4b451b8

entry.title: [gpustack] GPUStack: Authentication bypass via trusted loopback source (reverse-proxy TCP peer or X-GPUStack-Real-IP header) grants unauthenticated admin
entry.content:
Impact

In GPUStack before v2.2.0, get_current_user (in gpustack/api/auth.py) promotes any request whose source is considered loopback to the built-in administrator account when force_auth_localhost is False (the default). The "source" is derived by client_ip_getter, which can be made to report 127.0.0.1 without any credentials in two ways:

  1. Same-host reverse proxy (TCP peer). In the canonical self-hosted shape — GPUStack behind a same-host reverse proxy with proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:<port> — every remote request arrives at GPUStack with TCP peer 127.0.0.1, so the loopback auto-admin branch fires. No header or credential is required. Verified end-to-end against HEAD 6bee5883.
  2. X-GPUStack-Real-IP header. A forged X-GPUStack-Real-IP: 127.0.0.1 header can cause the request source to be treated as loopback.

Either path yields full, unauthenticated administrative access over the network: enumerate and modify users, models, workers, and configuration; mint persistent admin API keys (scope ["*"], valid from any source IP thereafter); read worker credentials and cloud/provider secrets. Combined with admin-only functionality such as POST /v2/inference-backends/from yaml, this leads to code execution on worker hosts.

This vulnerability has been observed exploited in the wild against a v2.1.1 deployment (attacker-created custom backends running reverse shells).

Root cause

Trusting the network source of a request (socket peer, or a client-controllable header) as an authentication signal. When GPUStack is fronted by a same-host reverse proxy, the socket peer is always loopback, so the "localhost is trusted" assumption no longer holds.

Patches

Fixed in gpustack 2.2.0: the loopback auto-admin path was removed and client-IP / forwarding-header handling was hardened. Upgrade to 2.2.0 or later.

Workarounds

  • Set force_auth_localhost=true to require authentication even for loopback requests.
  • Ensure the reverse proxy / gateway cannot cause GPUStack to treat external traffic as loopback, and strip any client-supplied X-GPUStack-Real-IP header at the edge.
  • Keep the API off untrusted networks (VPN / edge authentication).

Remediation (in the fix)

Do not derive authentication from the request's network source. Remove implicit loopback-based admin, and only accept a real client-IP header from an authenticated/trusted gateway (never from arbitrary clients).

Credit

entry.title: [djust] djust: A template binding inherits a context safety grant it never earned (XSS)
entry.content:
A context safety grant was inherited by a template binding that never earned it, so rebinding a name the view had marked safe left the mark attached to the new, attacker-controlled value.

djust's context safety channel is keyed by name, not by value. Every bind copied the value and left the grant in place:

view marks   p = mark_safe('<b>trusted</b>')
template     {% with p=user_input %}{{ p }}{% endwith %}

  djust   '<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>'          <- executes
  django  '<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>'

Affected binds

Eight distinct shapes were live. All are fixed in 1.1.2:

shape example
{% with %} rebinding a marked name {% with p=hostile %}{{ p }}{% endwith %}
{% with %} descendant of a rebound name {% with p=hostile %}{{ p.a }}{% endwith %}
{% with %} binding over a marked name {% with q=hostile %}{{ q }}{% endwith %}
{% for %} loop variable {% for p in hostiles %}{{ p }}{% endfor %}
{% for %} descendant {% for p in hostiles %}{{ p.a }}{% endfor %}
{% for %} tuple unpacking {% for k, v in rows %}{{ v }}{% endfor %}
{% include … with %} {% include "c.html" with q=hostile %}
assign tags {% … as x %}

No filter chain and no |safe anywhere in the template is required. The precondition is that the application marked some value safe under a name that a template later rebinds — an ordinary pattern, since a view commonly marks trusted markup safe and templates commonly reuse short names such as p, item or row.

Impact

Stored or reflected XSS in any djust application that combines mark_safe (or any framework path that grants a context key safety) with a template that rebinds that name. Exploitation requires no unusual template construct.

Patches

Fixed in 1.1.2, and in 1.2.0 (main).

The rule is that a bind replaces the grant rather than inheriting one. It is stated that way deliberately: the originally reported defects pointed the opposite direction — a grant being lost across some binds, causing over-escaping — and fixing only the reported direction would have left this leak in place. Both directions are the same rule.

Not fixed in 1.1.2, and tracked for 1.2.0: two over-escaping cases where a grant fails to travel with a value that legitimately carries one ({% with body=post.text|linebreaks %}, and mark_safe reaching a template through dict.values / dict.items). Both escape more than Django rather than less, so neither is a leak.

Workarounds

Before upgrading, avoid reusing a context name for both mark_safe'd content and untrusted input, and avoid rebinding such a name in {% with %}, {% for %}, {% include … with %} or an assign tag.

Credit

Found while preparing the 1.1.1 security release: the reproducer published in GHSA-9395-2g46-rj3f was run against the built 1.1.1 artifact before that advisory was published, and proved the class was still live. Publishing the original text would have reported this class as patched when it was not.

entry.title: [urwid] Urwid: handle_short_request() crashes on non-ASCII POST body (UnicodeEncodeError DoS)
entry.content:
Summary

The handle_short_request() function in urwid/display/web.py raises an unhandled UnicodeEncodeError when processing a POST request body containing non-ASCII bytes. The function reads POST input and encodes it to ASCII before writing to a named pipe. Any byte value above 0x7F causes the CGI process to exit with an unhandled exception, returning an HTTP 500 error to the client. Additionally, a file descriptor opened earlier in the same function is not closed before the exception propagates, causing a file descriptor leak for the lifetime of the CGI process.

A second instance of missing exception handling exists in the polling update path, where non-UTF-8 socket output causes an unhandled UnicodeDecodeError.

Impact

An attacker who observes a valid X-Urwid-ID session token (transmitted in plaintext HTTP response headers) can send repeated POST requests containing non-ASCII bytes to the urwid CGI endpoint. Each malformed request causes the CGI handler to crash with HTTP 500. This results in a Denial of Service (DoS) for legitimate users using the urwid web interface.

Affected Versions

urwid <= 4.0.6

Patches

Fixed in urwid 4.0.7. Users should upgrade to version 4.0.7 or later.

Workarounds

No direct workaround exists short of disabling the urwid web display interface.

entry.title: [fast-agent-mcp] fast-agent: `fast-agent serve` binds HTTP to 0.0.0.0 with no authentication by default; with --shell this is unauthenticated remote command execution
entry.content:
Summary

fast-agent serve exposes the agent over MCP. By default it uses HTTP transport bound to 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces) on port 8000 with no authentication (auth=None) and prints no warning. Any host that can reach the port can call the exposed agent tool. When the server is started with --shell (which is -x, the flag used in the README quickstart uvx fast-agent mcp@latest -x), the agent has a local execute shell tool, so an unauthenticated remote client can drive the agent into running arbitrary OS commands — unauthenticated RCE.

Affected code

  • cli/commands/serve.py — transport defaults to HTTP; --host defaults to 0.0.0.0; port 8000.
  • mcp/server/agent_server.py — auth_provider = None unless FAST_AGENT_SERVE_OAUTH=huggingface; run_async(transport="http", host=host, ...) with host defaulting to 0.0.0.0.
  • tools/local_shell_executor.py — the shell tool runs commands via create_subprocess_shell.

Verified (live, faithful — published 0.7.20 in Docker python:3.13-slim, stock unauthenticated client)

  1. Unauthenticated exposure (core defect): a client with no Authorization header completed initialize and tools/list (-> ['agent']) against http://HOST:8000/mcp. Model-independent.
  2. Unauthenticated RCE with --shell, demonstrated two ways:
    • Real production model (gpt-4o-mini): a single plain-language message asking the agent to run a command via its shell tool -> the model autonomously called execute and the command output (process identity showing it ran as root, the hostname, and the first lines of a sensitive system file) was returned to the unauthenticated caller.
    • Key-free deterministic (passthrough model): the tool-call directive invoked the shell tool directly, same result. The server-side permission prompt did not block this in non-interactive serve mode.

Proof of concept

Environment: Docker python:3.13-slim, pip install fast-agent-mcp -> 0.7.20.

# server (real model + the documented shell flag; 0.0.0.0 is also the built-in default)
OPENAI_API_KEY=*** fast-agent serve --model gpt-4o-mini --shell --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
#  -> "Uvicorn running on http://0.0.0.0:8000"   (no auth, no warning)

# attacker: unauthenticated MCP HTTP client (NO Authorization header) to http://HOST:8000/mcp
#   initialize()                       -> 200 OK (server fast-agent-MCP-Server 0.7.20)
#   tools/list                         -> ['agent']
#   tools/call name="agent" arguments={"message":
#       "Using your execute/shell tool, run exactly this command and return its raw stdout: "
#       "id; echo PWNED=$(hostname); cat /etc/passwd | head -2"}
#
# response returned to the UNAUTHENTICATED caller:
#   uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
#   PWNED=<host>
#   <first lines of /etc/passwd>

Also reproduced key-free with --model passthrough and the message ***CALL_TOOL execute {"command":"id"} (passthrough invokes the tool deterministically). Full transcript + client scripts were sent by email.

Impact

An unauthenticated client that can reach the serve port controls the agent: with --shell this is remote command execution as the server user; without --shell it is unauthenticated use of the operator's LLM and any configured MCP servers' tools. The 0.0.0.0 default makes the server reachable beyond localhost as soon as it runs on a non-isolated host. Preconditions (serve + shell) are noted above and are why I defer the exact rating to you.

Remediation

  1. Default the bind host to 127.0.0.1; require an explicit --host 0.0.0.0 opt-in for non-loopback.
  2. Print a loud warning when binding a non-loopback interface without authentication.

entry.title: [zizmor] zizmor: Debug logging prints available GitHub credentials in cleartext
entry.content:
Summary

zizmor 1.27.0 exposes GitHub access tokens in cleartext when debug-level logging is enabled. Tokens supplied via environment variables (GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, ZIZMOR_GITHUB_TOKEN), or the corresponding command-line options (--gh-token, --github-token, --zizmor-github-token) are included in the debug representation of the parsed application configuration and written to stderr.

The affected logging is enabled by a single -v/--verbose or an applicable RUST_LOG directive.

Details

The issue was introduced in commit 919bea46, merged through PR #2180. Version 1.26.1 and earlier are unaffected. Version 1.27.0 is the first and only affected release.

zizmor accepts GitHub credentials to perform authenticated GitHub API requests for the purposes of retrieving remote GitHub repositories and performing online audits that may require resolving information such as action references, commits, or repository metadata. A GitHub credential is used to avoid unauthenticated API limits and, when applicable, provide access to private repositories.

PR #2180 was intended to improve the experience around zizmor’s implicit offline mode. It also moved the CLI types into a dedicated module and added a debug log of the fully parsed App value:

tracing::debug!("app: {app:?}");

This diagnostic is useful for understanding the effective CLI state, including whether offline operation was explicit or inferred. However, the same commit added derived Debug implementations to App, NetworkArgs, and GitHubToken(String). Before the debug event is emitted, the compatibility token aliases are merged into app.network.gh_token.

The resulting stderr contains the token verbatim. Explicit --offline clears the token before the debug event, but normal online operation and --no-online-audits retain it.

PoC

Using zizmor at v1.27.0:

GH_TOKEN=gho_ZIZMOR_MRE zizmor --verbose example.yml

will emit

DEBUG zizmor: app: App { input: InputArgs { inputs: ["example.yml"], collect: [Default], strict_collection: false }, audit: AuditArgs { fix: None, pedantic: false, persona: Regular, min_severity: None, min_confidence: None, no_ignores: false }, output: OutputArgs { verbose: Verbosity { verbose: 1, quiet: 0, phantom: PhantomData<clap_verbosity_flag::InfoLevel> }, format: Plain, no_progress: false, color: None, render_links: Auto, show_audit_urls: Auto, no_exit_codes: false, naches: false }, network: NetworkArgs { offline: false, gh_token: Some(GitHubToken("gho_ZIZMOR_MRE")), github_token: None, zizmor_github_token: None, gh_hostname: Standard("github.com"), no_online_audits: false, cache_dir: "/Users/shaan/.cache/zizmor" }, args: GlobalArgs { lsp: LspArgs { lsp: false, stdio: false }, config: None, no_config: false, completions: None, thanks: false, help: (), version: () } }

Impact

In practice, the impact of this vulnerability should be mediated by GitHub's own layered defenses, including secret redaction in Actions logs and automatic credential revocation in issue/PR/etc. comments. However, zizmor itself should never log sensitive materials, and so the behavior is still considered vulnerable even if compensating controls exist in downstream systems.

An affected user must enable debug logging while supplying a GitHub credential, and the resulting stderr must be available to another party. Plausible disclosure channels include a public bug report, CI log or artifact, or terminal capture. A potential attacker only needs permission to read the disclosed logs.

The resulting impact depends on the token's scopes, repository access, and lifetime. A minimally scoped token may only expose public read-only data, while a broader OAuth token or personal access token may permit private-repository or modification of repositories, packages, workflows, or organization resources. The default informational logging level is unaffected. Exploitation requires debug logging and subsequent log exposure, which limits likelihood.

Notably, because zizmor’s bug-report template asks users to rerun commands with --verbose and paste the complete logs, this can result in credentials being copied into public issues or other support channels.
